summaries.summary: The newly landed "entitlements engine" is a **boolean feature-flag system, not a quota engine**. `feature_registry.py` defines 27 features with only `key/label/category/description/gateable` — there is no numeric limit field anywhere. `EntitlementService` resolves a single global blob `{"kill": {key: bool}, "matrix": {family: {key: bool}}}` from `feature_flags` + the new `plan_features` table, caches it in-process for 60s, and answers `has_feature(key, user)` → bool. Enforcement is applied via `require_feature(key)` / `require_feature_optional(key)` FastAPI dependencies attached to ~40 individual routes. There are **no counters, no usage rows, no reset window, no INCR, no SELECT FOR UPDATE** in this engine — the concurrency questions are moot because nothing is ever counted. Migration `0035_admin_control_plane.py` seeds every (plan_family × gateable feature) row to `enabled=True` and every kill-switch to `true`, so in the shipped state the engine denies nothing; I confirmed this live: `GET http://localhost:8030/config/entitlements` as an anonymous caller returns all 27 features `true`. Critically, the prior audit's gap is **not closed**: `SUBSCRIPTION_PLANS` in `config.py` still advertises `free: {compilations: 3, optimizations: 0}` and `get_plan_config()` is referenced only from `payment_service.py` (checkout/display) — never from any enforcement path. The primary product flow (`POST /jobs/submit` with `job_type` in `latex_compilation|llm_optimization|combined`) carries no `require_feature` dependency at all, and `sync_has_feature()` (the worker-side hook) is dead code called from nowhere, so neither the `llm_optimize` kill-switch nor the plan matrix can reach the main LLM path. Money-spending route inventory: **gated by feature flag (but never quota'd)** — `/optimize`, `/optimize-and-compile`, `/jobs/batch`, `/ats/score`, `/ats/quick-score`, `/ats/deep-analyze`, `/ats/semantic-match`, `/cover-letters/generate`, `/career/analyze`, `/interview/…generate`, `/byok/generate`, `/ai/generate-bullets`, `/ai/generate-summary`, `/ai/rewrite`, `/ai/proofread|translate`; **completely ungated** — `POST /jobs/submit` (all four job types incl. LLM), `POST /resumes/{id}/quick-tailor`, `POST /resumes/{id}/academic-cv-convert`, `POST /compile`, `POST /ai/salary-estimate`, `POST /ai/reorder-sections`, `POST /ai/explain-error`.

The Admin Control Plane adds a `users.role` column (user|support|admin), a `plan_features` (plan_family × feature_key) matrix table, and per-feature kill-switch rows in `feature_flags` (migration 0035). `backend/app/api/admin_routes.py` exposes one public route (`GET /config/feature-flags`, filtered through a PUBLIC_FLAG_KEYS allowlist) and seven admin routes: list/patch feature flags, get entitlement state, patch kill-switch, patch matrix cell, list users, and patch a user's role. Every one of the seven admin routes carries `Depends(require_admin)` — I verified against the live OpenAPI spec that no other `/admin/*` path exists unguarded, and curled all of them unauthenticated (all 401). `require_admin` in `auth_middleware.py` resolves the Better Auth session to a user_id, then reads `SELECT email, role, email_verified FROM users`, granting access on `role == 'admin'` OR (email ∈ ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_EMAILS AND email_verified); it deliberately refuses the legacy JWT `is_admin` claim and returns 503 (not 403) on DB failure. There is no privilege escalation reachable from a non-admin session: no other code path writes `users.role`, and the role field is not mass-assignable from any profile endpoint. The real defects are elsewhere: a startup reconcile in `main.py` promotes ADMIN_EMAIL matches to `role='admin'` with no email-verification check, silently undoing the very safeguard `require_admin` documents; there is zero audit logging for any admin mutation; the `support` role is a stub that only grants a free entitlement bypass; and the admin nav link is still gated on a build-time env var rather than the new RBAC role, so promoting a user via the new Users tab has no UI effect. The error-envelope passthrough in `core/errors.py` is correct and is what makes the frontend's `last_admin` 409 detection work.

The auth-completion drop layers three things on top of Better Auth 1.6.9 running inside the Next.js app at /api/auth/[...all]: (1) a provider-agnostic transactional email sender (frontend/src/lib/email.ts) that posts to Resend when RESEND_API_KEY is set and otherwise console-logs the whole email; (2) Better Auth config in frontend/src/lib/auth.ts that enables emailAndPassword with sendResetPassword, emailVerification with sendOnSignUp + autoSignInAfterVerification, an in-memory IP rate limiter, and conditionally-registered Google/GitHub social providers; (3) three new client pages (/forgot-password, /reset-password, /verify-email) plus a dismissible EmailVerifyBanner mounted in the root layout. Password-reset tokens are Better Auth's DB-backed generateId(24) values (≈143 bits, single-use via deleteVerificationByIdentifier, 1h expiry, looked up by exact identifier) — that part is sound. Email-verification tokens are stateless HS256 JWTs over {email} signed with BETTER_AUTH_SECRET; replay after verification is harmless because the handler early-returns once emailVerified is true. Open redirect is covered: every callbackURL/redirectTo passes through Better Auth's originCheck against trustedOrigins with relative paths allowed. Verification is deliberately soft — nothing in the frontend or backend gates functionality on emailVerified except the ADMIN_EMAIL match path in backend/app/middleware/auth_middleware.py:306, which correctly requires it. The defects are concentrated in the glue code this drop added: a verify-email callback that renders success as failure, an email sender that silently degrades to logging secrets, sessions surviving a password reset, and a defeated timing-attack mitigation.

packages/tui is a published npm CLI (`@sanskarpan/latexy`, bin `latexy`) built with Ink + React 18 + nanostores, bundled by tsup into a single ESM `dist/cli.js` with a `#!/usr/bin/env node` banner. `src/cli.tsx` branches on TTY/`CI`/`--json`: non-TTY goes to `src/headless.ts` (only `compile` is implemented, JSON-on-stdout, exit codes 0/1/2/3), otherwise it renders `App` → `AppShell`. `src/lib/api-client.ts` is a fetch wrapper with 3-attempt retry, 30s timeout, and Bearer auth; `src/lib/ws-client.ts` is a `ws`-based client that connects to `/ws/jobs`, unwraps the `{type:"event",event:{...}}` envelope, buffers-then-drains, and reconnects with exponential backoff. `src/lib/config.ts` persists a TOML config at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/latexy/config.toml` with mode 0600 (that part is sound; `LATEXY_SESSION_TOKEN` overrides the on-disk token). The command layer registers 32 slash commands in `registry.ts` but `dispatch.ts` only implements 7. Cross-checking against the live backend: the REST paths (`/me`, `/health`, `/resumes/`, `/resumes/{id}`, `/jobs/submit`, `/download/{id}`, `DELETE /jobs/{id}`) all exist and the request/response shapes line up — but the two things that make the CLI usable, WebSocket auth and interactive login, are both broken against the current backend, so in practice no authenticated compile ever completes and there is no way to log in interactively.

The TUI is an Ink v5 + React 18 terminal client for Latexy, published as `@sanskarpan/latexy`. State lives in four nanostores atoms (`$messages`, `$overlay`, `$session`, `$ui`); `AppShell` composes `StatusBar` / `TranscriptView` / overlay slot / `PromptInput` / `KeyboardHints`, and a global `useWSEventRouter` fans WebSocket events into per-job `JobController` instances that mutate `$messages`. Slash input is tokenized by `commands/parser.ts` and dispatched through two handler tables in `commands/dispatch.ts`. `cli.tsx` branches to a headless JSON path when stdout is not a TTY or `--json` is passed. Credential handling in `LoginOverlay` is correct on the sensitive point — the password field uses `mask="*"` and is cleared on failure, config is written `0o600`, and `theme.ts` emits plain chalk color names so `NO_COLOR`/non-TTY degrade normally (and non-TTY never reaches the renderer anyway). Long log lines are handled with `wrap="truncate-end"`, so wide/long output is safe. The serious problems are elsewhere: the transcript uses Ink `<Static>` with a non-append-only array so streaming log updates and the tool-completion row are lost or duplicated; the job-completion handler dereferences a field the backend never emits and the resulting TypeError is swallowed by an empty `catch {}` in the WS client; the prompt input is unmounted while a job runs so the `/cancel` the UI advertises cannot be typed; the login overlay POSTs to a route that 404s on the configured backend; and 25 of the 32 registered/documented slash commands have no handler at all.

Ingestion is a factory of 11 parser classes (`backend/app/parsers/`) mapped onto 12 `ResumeFormat` enum values by `ParserFactory._register_parsers()` (DOC reuses `DOCXParser`). Every registered format is also present in `FormatDetectionService.FORMAT_CONFIG` and every extension is in the UI's `ACCEPTED_EXTENSIONS`, so no parser is orphaned by registration — but `TextParser` is unreachable in practice because the YAML heuristic in `detect_format_from_content` claims most plain-text resumes first (proven live). `backend/app/api/format_routes.py` exposes six routes; `/detect`, `/validate`, `/parse` and the LaTeX branch of `/upload` are fully unauthenticated, and `/upload` requires auth only for the LLM branch. Format is sniffed from content first (good — extension/MIME are only fallbacks) and a 10 MB streaming read cap exists. XXE is handled: `XMLParser` uses `defusedxml`, `python-docx` sets `resolve_entities=False`, and mammoth's minidom/expat now rejects entity amplification (verified against installed packages). There is no zip-slip risk (nothing is extracted to disk) and filenames are never used as paths. What is missing is any decompression-ratio limit on DOCX, any offloading of the CPU/memory-heavy parse work off the event loop, and any entitlement/quota gate on the LLM conversion path.

Four integrations live in `backend/app/api/{github,dropbox,zotero,mendeley}_routes.py`, each with a `/connect` → provider → `/callback` OAuth dance and per-resume push/pull (GitHub, Dropbox) or per-resume BibTeX import (Zotero, Mendeley). GitHub/Dropbox tokens are stored in dedicated `users` columns; Zotero/Mendeley tokens live in the `users.user_metadata` JSON blob. All tokens are encrypted with `EncryptionService` (Fernet), which now hard-fails at construction if a real Fernet key is absent in staging/production, so the previously-reported fixed PBKDF2 salt is confined to dev/test and is no longer a production issue. CSRF `state` nonces are generated with `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, stored in Redis with a 10-minute TTL keyed to the initiating `user_id`, and single-use-deleted on callback; `redirect_uri` is always taken from server config, never from the request, so there is no open redirect. Every push/pull/import/status endpoint filters `Resume.user_id == user_id`, so cross-user resume access is correctly blocked, and Dropbox/Mendeley both implement lazy refresh-on-401 with a useful "reconnect in Settings" error. `job_scraper_service.py` has a real SSRF guard (`_assert_public_url` plus a `_SSRFGuardTransport` that re-validates every redirect hop) — I confirmed live that `169.254.169.254`, `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are all rejected. The defects that remain are: the callbacks are completely unauthenticated and never bind the completing browser to the state's user (classic account-linking CSRF), the scraper's rate limiter unconditionally trusts `X-Forwarded-For` while the rest of the codebase gates that behind `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS`, one GitHub OAuth app is shared by two flows with different callback URLs, Dropbox per-resume state is missing from the resume API response so the editor UI can never restore it, and every OAuth error redirect the backend emits is ignored by the settings page.

There are four independent "multi-user" systems that share no common membership model. (1) Team workspaces (`/workspaces`, backend/app/api/workspace_routes.py) — owner-only admin, members resolved by existing account email, no invite token or acceptance step; member rows carry an `editor|viewer` role that is written and rendered but never read for any authorization decision. (2) Team billing seats (`/team`, team_routes.py) — the only surface with a real invite token: a 7-day Redis token bound to the invited email, deleted on use; accepting flips the member's `subscription_plan` to `team_member`. (3) White-label tenants (`/tenants`, tenant_routes.py + middleware/tenant_middleware.py) — creation is completely ungated (any authenticated free user may create 10 tenants), invites instantly add any user by email with no consent and no way to leave, and `custom_domain` is self-asserted with `POST /{id}/domain/verify` being a pure instructions stub that never checks DNS. TenantMiddleware resolves a tenant from `X-Tenant-Slug` or Host and attaches it to `request.state.tenant`, but the only consumer in the entire codebase is `GET /tenants/current-context`; no query anywhere is scoped by tenant, so "tenant isolation" does not exist to be crossed. (4) Realtime collaboration (`/ws/collab/{resume_id}` + services/collab_manager.py) — a Y.js relay whose room registry is a process-local dict, with permission checked once at connect and never re-checked. Comments (comment_routes.py) are workspace-scoped only and their UI component is not mounted anywhere. The entitlement engine reads the user's plan fresh per call, so there is no stale-entitlement cache — but plan state itself is left inconsistent when a team owner's subscription ends.

The editor page (frontend/src/app/workspace/[resumeId]/edit/page.tsx, 3077 lines) renders a fixed three-column desktop layout: a collapsible outline aside, a flex:3 editor section, a mouse-only drag handle, and a right aside with 17 tabs pinned to minWidth 340px. The only "responsive" behaviour in the whole page is a `matchMedia('(max-width: 768px)')` flag that swaps Monaco (LaTeXEditor.tsx) for a CodeMirror-based MobileEditor.tsx inside that same unchanged desktop layout. MobileEditor implements the LaTeXEditorRef contract but stubs out 9 of its 13 methods as no-ops. GlobalHeader.tsx was recently hardened (Escape handler, aria-expanded/aria-haspopup, aria-labels, offline-data purge on sign-out) and is now one of the better components; the rest of the app has no focus trapping anywhere and inconsistent dialog semantics. Root layout.tsx is light — Monaco and react-pdf are behind next/dynamic on the editor page — but react-pdf pulls its worker from a third-party CDN, and MobileEditor's CodeMirror bundle is statically imported for desktop users too. The PWA service worker is generated from next.config.js `runtimeCaching`; two of its three route regexes cannot match the URLs the app actually requests. KeyboardShortcutsPanel.tsx renders a 24-entry catalogue from lib/editor-shortcuts.ts, but only three shortcuts are actually bound anywhere in the codebase.

Anonymous/trial compiles must use /public/compile ... this endpoint must never be an open, unmetered pdflatex execution path."` — yet the far more expensive LLM route next to it is exactly that.
confirmed.impact: Anyone on the internet can drain the platform OpenAI budget without an account, a device fingerprint, or a trial record. The only brake is the generic per-IP RateLimitMiddleware (60/min, 1000/hr) which itself fails open when Redis is down (`middleware/rate_limiting.py:117-120`). 1000 gpt-4-class completions per hour per IP, trivially parallelised across IPs.

Against the running stack, six consecutive anonymous calls all returned HTTP 200 with real LLM output:
`for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST http://localhost:8030/optimize -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"latex_content":"\\documentclass{article}\\begin{document}Engineer\\end{document}","job_description":"software engineer"}'; done` → `200 200 200 200 200 200`, body contains a fully rewritten LaTeX resume.

confirmed.correction: Core defect confirmed: POST /optimize and POST /optimize-and-compile are reachable with no session, no device fingerprint and no trial record, and execute an LLM call on the platform OpenAI key via the llm_service singleton, bypassing the per-identity platform-key meter used by ai_routes. /optimize-and-compile additionally invokes pdflatex, contradicting the stated policy in /compile's own docstring. Corrections to the claimed impact: (1) the default model is gpt-4o-mini (config.py:100), not a gpt-4-class model, and output tokens are capped, so per-call cost is cents-scale; (2) the binding brake is RATE_LIMIT_CALLS_PER_MINUTE=60 against a spoof-resistant client id, not 1000/hr, plus BodySizeLimitMiddleware on prompt size — the Redis fail-open at rate_limiting.py:117-120 is a pre-existing global property, not specific to these routes; (3) no frontend code calls either endpoint (zero grep hits in frontend/src), so these appear to be orphaned legacy routes — still publicly exposed, but safe to gate behind _require_user or delete outright. Severity is better characterised as high (unauthenticated cost/DoS vector on an unused legacy route) than critical.

confirmed.title: POST /jobs/submit — the primary LLM+compile path — has no entitlement gate, and the worker-side hook sync_has_feature() is dead code
confirmed.evidence:
```

async def submit_job(
    request: JobSubmissionRequest,
    http_request: Request,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    user_id: Optional[str] = Depends(get_current_user_optional),

```
No `dependencies=[Depends(require_feature(...))]`. The only enforcement in the body is the anonymous device trial, guarded by `if user_id is None and request.job_type in _TRIAL_JOB_TYPES:`. The comment at line 262 asserts a guarantee that does not exist in code:

```
# their plan, but anonymous callers must pass the device trial here
```
Nothing downstream reads the plan for anything except queue priority and compile timeout (`_resolve_user_plan` → `estimated_time`, `safe_model`).

The worker fallback is never wired: `rg -n 'sync_has_feature' app` matches only its definition in entitlement_service.py:283 and its own docstring. No Celery task (llm_worker, orchestrator, ats_worker, latex_worker) calls it.
confirmed.impact: The `llm_optimize` kill-switch and the whole plan matrix are unenforceable on the flow the product actually uses: the frontend's optimize action calls `submitJob({job_type: 'combined', ...})` (frontend/src/lib/api-client.ts:1314-1315). An admin flipping `llm_optimize` off globally during a cost incident would block `/optimize` and `/ai/*` but the real traffic through `/jobs/submit` would keep spending. Authenticated free users get unlimited combined optimize+compile jobs.
confirmed.repro: Read job_routes.py:243 — no require_feature dependency. Then `rg -n 'sync_has_feature' backend/app` → only the definition. Submit `POST /jobs/submit {"job_type":"llm_optimization", "latex_content":"..."}` while authenticated as a free user; it queues regardless of the entitlement matrix.
confirmed.fix: Attach a per-job-type entitlement check inside submit_job (e.g. `if request.job_type in {'llm_optimization','combined'} and not await entitlement_service.has_feature('llm_optimize', user=user_id): raise 403`, `ats_scoring` → `ats_score`), and either call `sync_has_feature` in the workers as a second line of defence or delete it.
confirmed.correction: Corrected claim (severity: medium, not high): POST /jobs/submit and POST /jobs/compile-watermarked carry no entitlement dependency, so the admin kill-switch and per-plan matrix for llm_optimize, ats_score, and ats_deep are bypassable on the app's primary traffic path, while /optimize, /optimize-and-compile, and /ai/* are correctly gated. Verified live: with kill.llm_optimize=false, /optimize returned 403 feature_disabled and /jobs/submit {job_type:"combined"} returned 200 with the job reaching "processing" in the worker. Real impact is a broken cost/incident control and a routable-around per-plan gate — NOT "authenticated free users get unlimited combined jobs": entitlements are boolean access with no metering anywhere for authenticated users, migration 0035 seeds every (plan_family x gateable feature) as enabled, and volume is still bounded by RateLimitMiddleware (60/min, 1000/hr keyed on session token or IP). The sync_has_feature "dead code" sub-claim is factually correct but is unused, fail-open, documented worker plumbing — it is not what causes the bypass; the missing route-level dependency is. The misleading comment at job_routes.py:261-265 ("authenticated users are governed by their plan") should be corrected along with the fix.

confirmed.title: Last-admin guard is a TOCTOU check-then-write: concurrent demotions can drive the admin count to zero
confirmed.impact: With exactly two admins, two concurrent PATCH requests each demoting a different admin both observe admin_count == 2, both pass the guard, and both commit — leaving zero admins. Every /admin/* endpoint then returns 403 for everyone, and the only recovery paths are direct DB access or adding an email to ADMIN_EMAIL plus a backend restart. The same pattern also allows a double-submit on a single admin's own demotion to interleave with another concurrent demotion.
confirmed.repro:
1. Seed exactly two admins A and B.
2. Fire both requests simultaneously from an authenticated admin session: `PATCH /admin/users/{A}/role {"role":"user"}` and `PATCH /admin/users/{B}/role {"role":"user"}` (e.g. two curl processes started together, or `xargs -P2`).
3. `select count(*) from users where role='admin'` → 0. All subsequent /admin/* calls return 403 "Admin privileges required".
confirmed.fix: Serialize the invariant: take a transaction-scoped advisory lock (`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(<const>)`) before the count, or re-count with `SELECT ... FROM users WHERE role='admin' FOR UPDATE` so concurrent demotions block, and perform the count and the UPDATE in the same transaction.
confirmed.correction: The last-admin guard is indeed a TOCTOU check-then-write (no FOR UPDATE, no lock, no DB constraint, READ COMMITTED), and two concurrent PATCHes demoting two different admins can drive users.role='admin' to zero. But the impact is much smaller than claimed: ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_EMAILS is the only bootstrap path for role='admin' (backend/app/main.py:48-70), so it is always configured wherever admins exist, and require_admin grants admin on the verified-email path independently of the role column -- the bootstrap admin never loses access. Recovery is a plain backend restart (the startup reconcile re-promotes), not direct DB access or a config change. Requires an already-authenticated admin issuing deliberately concurrent demotions of two distinct admin rows; the admin UI has no bulk role change. Severity: low. Fix is a one-liner: add .with_for_update() to the target-row load (or lock the admin rows) before counting.

```
if (ctx.context.options.emailAndPassword?.revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset)
```

confirmed.title: OAuth error path permanently locks the whole sign-in/sign-up form

confirmed.title: Rate limiting on forgot-password / resend-verification uses in-memory storage on a serverless deploy
confirmed.evidence:
```
rateLimit: {
  enabled: true,
  window: 60,
  max: 20,
  storage: 'memory',
},
```
better-auth/dist/api/rate-limiter/index.mjs:78-95 implements `storage === 'memory'` as a module-level `const memory = new Map()`, and keys entries by `createRateLimitKey(ip, path)` only. The stricter defaults that actually protect these endpoints live in the same per-process Map (getDefaultSpecialRules(): `path === "/request-password-reset" || path === "/send-verification-email"` → `window: 60, max: 3`). frontend/.env.production.example's header says the target is Vercel ("These go into Vercel dashboard → Project Settings → Environment Variables"), and frontend/vercel.json confirms it.

An attacker who can fan out requests (or simply rotate source IPs, since the key is IP-only) can drive a large volume of password-reset and verification emails to a victim's inbox and burn the Resend send quota. confirmed.title: WS client sends the session token as an Authorization header, but /ws/jobs only reads ?token= — every subscribe to an owned job is rejected, and the rejection is silently discarded
confirmed.evidence:
TUI: `this.ws = new WS(this.url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${this.token}` } })` and the URL is built as `backendUrl.replace(/^http/, 'ws') + '/ws/jobs'` (app.tsx:22, headless.ts:47) — no `?token=` is ever appended.

Backend `backend/app/api/ws_routes.py:163-175`:
```python
async def _resolve_ws_user(websocket: WebSocket) -> Optional[str]:
    token = websocket.query_params.get("token")
    if not token:
        return None
```
and `_job_ws_access_ok` → `return job_owner is None or job_owner == user_id`.

The TUI then throws the resulting error frame away: `} else if (outer['type'] === 'subscribed') {...}  // Other outer types (heartbeat, error) are intentionally ignored` and the whole handler is wrapped in `try { ... } catch {}`.

The frontend does it correctly — `frontend/src/lib/ws-client.ts:46`: "Better Auth session token, forwarded as ?token= so the backend can authorize access to the user's own (owner-scoped) jobs."
confirmed.impact: Every job submitted via `/jobs/submit` while authenticated gets `meta.user_id` set (`backend/app/api/job_routes.py:186-192`), so `_job_ws_access_ok` returns False for the TUI's always-anonymous connection. The server replies `{"type":"error","code":"forbidden"}`, which the client ignores. Result: no `log.line`, `job.progress`, `job.completed` or `job.failed` ever reaches the CLI. Interactive `/compile` spins on "running" forever; `latexy compile --json` blocks the full 5 minutes and then exits 1 with "Job timed out after 5 minutes" even though the compile succeeded. The core feature of the package does not work.
confirmed.repro:
Proven live against the running backend:
```
docker exec latexy-redis redis-cli set "latexy:job:aud-test-1:meta" '{"job_id":"aud-test-1","user_id":"someuser"}' EX 300
# connect with Authorization header only, exactly as the TUI does:
websockets.connect("ws://localhost:8030/ws/jobs", additional_headers={"Authorization":"Bearer sometoken"})
send {"type":"subscribe","job_id":"aud-test-1","last_event_id":"0"}
```
Server response: `{"type":"error","code":"forbidden","message":"Access denied for this job"}`
confirmed.fix: In `LatexyWSClient.openSocket()`, append the token as a query param: `new WS(`${this.url}?token=${encodeURIComponent(this.token)}`)` (keep the header too if desired — the backend ignores it). Separately, stop swallowing `{type:"error"}`: emit it as an `error` event so `forbidden`/`rate_limited` surface to the user, and make `headless.ts` fail fast on a forbidden subscribe instead of waiting 5 minutes.
confirmed.correction: The finding is accurate as written. Only nuance: the failure is confined to the packages/tui CLI (the web frontend correctly appends ?token= at frontend/src/lib/ws-client.ts:146-147), and the server does log the forbidden rejection — it is the client that discards it. Fix is either appending the token as a query param in the TUI's openSocket() or adding an Authorization-header fallback in _resolve_ws_user.

confirmed.title: Interactive local-file compile posts to POST /compile expecting an async job with a WS stream, but that endpoint is fully synchronous and emits no events
confirmed.evidence:
```ts
const res = await client.postForm<JobSubmitResponse>('/compile', form)
const jobId = res.job_id
$activeJobId.set(jobId)
const ctrl = createJobController(jobId)
ctrl.setToolMsgId(toolMsgId)
wsClient.subscribe(jobId, '0')
```
with `interface JobSubmitResponse { job_id: string; status: string }`.

Backend `backend/app/api/routes.py:350-356` is a blocking call returning `CompilationResponse` (`success, job_id, message, compilation_time, pdf_size, log_output` — no `status`), and `latex_service.compile_latex` (`backend/app/services/latex_service.py:100`) never calls `publish_event`; the streaming variant is a different function (line ~234).

The form also sends a field the endpoint doesn't accept: `form.append('compiler', compiler)` — the signature is only `latex_content: Form(None), file: File(None)`.
confirmed.impact: `/compile some.tex` blocks for the whole synchronous compile, then subscribes to a job_id that has no Redis stream and no publisher. `$activeJobId` is set and never cleared, so the tool card spins forever and every subsequent `/compile` is refused with "A job is already running. Use /cancel to stop it first." The compiler flag is silently ignored (always pdflatex). The PDF that was actually produced is never surfaced.
confirmed.repro: In interactive mode with a valid token: `/compile ./resume.tex`. The card stays `running` indefinitely; a second `/compile` is rejected as "already running".
confirmed.fix: Read the local file and submit it through `POST /jobs/submit` with `job_type: 'latex_compilation'`, `latex_content`, `compiler` — exactly what `headless.ts:76-81` already does — instead of `POST /compile`. If `/compile` must be kept, treat it as synchronous: render the returned `CompilationResponse` directly and never call `wsClient.subscribe`.
confirmed.correction: Core defect is real; two details are overstated. (1) It does not block for an unbounded time: ApiClient.postForm uses timeoutMs = 30_000 with AbortSignal.timeout (api-client.ts:113-122), so compiles exceeding 30s abort into the catch block and correctly mark the tool card as error — and because $activeJobId.set(jobId) runs only after a successful await, the session wedge occurs specifically when the synchronous compile SUCCEEDS within 30s. (2) The wedge is per-session (restarting the TUI clears it), though there is no in-session recovery since /cancel also fails to clear $activeJobId. Everything else — no events, spinner never resolves, subsequent /compile refused, compiler flag silently ignored (FastAPI drops the unknown form field and pdflatex is hardcoded), produced PDF never surfaced — is accurate.

confirmed.title: JobController.onComplete dereferences ev.result, which the backend never emits — TypeError is swallowed by an empty catch, so the compile result card is never rendered
confirmed.evidence:
```ts
const result = ev.result as Record<string, unknown>
if (result['pdf_url'] != null || result['pages'] != null) {
```
`event-types.ts:52-54` itself marks `result?: Record<string, unknown>` as "Legacy / fallback". The real backend event is flat — `backend/app/workers/latex_worker.py:465-477` publishes `{"percent":100,"pdf_job_id":...,"ats_score":...,"compilation_time":...,"page_count":...,"compiler":...}` and `event_publisher.publish_event` builds `{event_id, job_id, timestamp, sequence, type, **payload_extra}` — there is no `result` key anywhere.

The resulting `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'pdf_url')` propagates out of `emit('event')` into `ws-client.ts`'s message handler, which is `try { ... } catch {}` — swallowed with no logging.
confirmed.impact: Even once the WS auth bug is fixed, a successful compile in interactive mode shows a tool card with `toolResult: undefined` and never renders the `CompileResultCard` (pages, size, ATS score, PDF URL). The throw also skips `controllers.delete(ev.job_id)` in the switch (`useJobStream.ts:141`), leaking the controller. No error is ever shown or logged.
confirmed.repro: Feed the router a real backend `job.completed` payload (flat, no `result`): `wsClient.emit('event', {type:'job.completed', job_id, page_count:2, ats_score:84, compilation_time:1.2, compiler:'pdflatex', ...})` → TypeError, no compile_result message added.
confirmed.fix: Read the flat fields the backend actually sends (as `headless.ts:100-107` already correctly does): `ev.page_count`, `ev.ats_score`, `ev.compilation_time`, `ev.compiler`, falling back to `ev.result?.[...]`. Replace the bare `catch {}` in `ws-client.ts` with something that at least records the error, so this class of bug is not invisible.
confirmed.correction: Core defect confirmed: `ev.result` is undefined for every real backend job.completed event, so `result['pdf_url']` throws a TypeError that ws-client.ts's empty catch swallows, CompileResultCard is never rendered, and controllers.delete(ev.job_id) is skipped (small per-job Map leak). Two refinements: (1) the throw occurs after `updateMessage(toolMsgId, {toolState:'success', ...})` and after `$activeJobId.set(null)`, so the tool card still shows success and the UI is not left stuck in a busy state — only the result card is lost; (2) merely defaulting `ev.result ?? {}` won't fix it, because job.completed carries pdf_job_id/page_count/ats_score/compilation_time/compiler flat and never carries pdf_url or size_bytes — those come from job.pdf_extracted, for which the router switch has no case. Correct fix: read the flat fields off the event and add a job.pdf_extracted handler. Severity medium-high rather than high.

confirmed.title: Headless --output writes the HTTP response body to the PDF file without checking res.ok, then reports success and exits 0
confirmed.impact: In CI, a 403/404 produces a file named e.g. `out.pdf` containing `{"error":{"code":"http_error",...}}`, the tool logs "PDF saved", prints `{"success": true, ...}` and exits 0. Downstream pipeline steps (artifact upload, email attachment) silently ship a corrupt PDF. This is the exact failure mode CI exit codes exist to prevent.
confirmed.repro: `LATEXY_SESSION_TOKEN=<valid> latexy compile --resume-id <uuid> --output out.pdf --json` against a job whose PDF has been cleaned up → `file out.pdf` reports JSON/ASCII text, exit code 0.
confirmed.fix: `if (!pdfRes.ok) { out({ success:false, error: `Download failed: ${pdfRes.status}` }); return 1 }` before reading the body, and additionally assert `Content-Type: application/pdf`.
confirmed.correction: Core defect confirmed but severity should be medium, not high. Corrected claim: packages/tui/src/headless.ts:92-99 writes the /download/{job_id} response body to --output without checking pdfRes.ok or content-type, then logs "PDF saved", prints {"success": true, ...} and exits 0. If the download returns 403 or 404 the tool writes a JSON error body into the .pdf and reports success — verified empirically (404 body is application/json, written file is 'JSON data'). Reachability is limited, though: the download is only attempted after a job.completed event, which the worker publishes solely on the success path immediately after caching the PDF in Redis (86400s TTL), using the same token that submitted the job seconds earlier. So 403 requires the session to expire mid-job, and 404 requires the best-effort Redis PDF cache write to have failed or the key to have been evicted (the filesystem fallback is unavailable because job_dir is always rmtree'd in the worker's finally block). It is a genuine missing-error-check bug that defeats CI exit codes under a degraded Redis, not a routine failure mode.

confirmed.impact: Compounds every other WS bug: `forbidden` (finding 1) and any exception thrown by a downstream listener (finding 4) vanish. The user sees a spinner that never resolves and has no way to diagnose. There is also no `subscribe` acknowledgement timeout, so a dropped/refused subscribe is indistinguishable from a slow job.
confirmed.repro: Any of finding 1's repro steps — the server error frame arrives on the socket and the CLI displays nothing.

confirmed.title: TranscriptView feeds a non-append-only array to Ink <Static>, so streaming log updates are frozen, completed tool rows are dropped, and cards are duplicated
confirmed.impact: Ink's <Static> is append-only: it keeps an internal `index` and renders `items.slice(index)`, advancing `index` to `items.length`. Two consequences on every /compile: (a) the `log_stream` message lands in `completed` immediately (it has neither `streaming` nor `toolState`), so it is emitted once with whatever lines it had at that instant and every later `updateMessage` is never re-rendered — the advertised "real-time streaming log output" shows only the first line; (b) when the running tool message flips to `toolState: 'success'` it is spliced into the MIDDLE of `completed` (it was added before the log message), shifting indices — Static then re-emits the log card as a duplicate and never renders the ✓ tool-completion row at all.
confirmed.repro: Trace the store: dispatch('/compile') → messages=[user]; completed len 1, Static index=1. runCompile adds tool_use running → completed still len 1 (active). First log.line adds log_stream → completed=[user, log], Static renders log, index=2. Subsequent log lines only call updateMessage → completed length stays 2 → Static renders nothing (log card frozen at 1 line). job.completed sets toolState='success' → completed=[user, tool, log], length 3 → Static renders slice(2)=[log] → log card printed a SECOND time, tool row never printed.
confirmed.fix: Do not derive Static's items by filtering a mutable list. Keep a separate, strictly append-only `finalized` array that a message is pushed onto exactly once (and never before it is terminal), or drop <Static> and render the full list with a bounded tail window.
confirmed.correction: The core defect is real and reproducible; two small precisions. (a) "shows only the first line" should be "freezes at whatever lines were in the store when React first flushed that Static item" — usually one line under React 18 batching, possibly a small burst. The full log does eventually surface, but only as a duplicate card emitted at completion, never as live streaming. confirmed.title: All parsers do blocking CPU work inside async handlers — one OCR upload freezes the entire event loop
confirmed.evidence:
format_routes.py:311 `parsed = await parser.parse(content, filename)` — but every `parse` is `async def` with purely synchronous bodies and no `run_in_threadpool`/`run_in_executor`:
image_parser.py:45 `text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img, lang='eng', config='--psm 6 --oem 3', timeout=OCR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)`
pdf_parser.py:36 `for page in pdf.pages[:MAX_PDF_PAGES]: text = page.extract_text(...)`
ocr_pdf_bytes() loops up to MAX_OCR_PAGES=10 pages at OCR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=30 each → up to 300 s of blocking work in one request.
confirmed.impact: POST /formats/parse and /formats/detect/validate are unauthenticated. A single 1.4 MB PNG makes the whole FastAPI process unresponsive for the OCR duration; a scanned PDF can hold it for ~5 minutes. Every other user's requests (compiles, auth, health checks) hang. The 60 req/min global rate limit does not help — one request is enough.
confirmed.repro:
Generate a 4000x5000 text-filled PNG, then:
curl -F "file=@big.png" http://localhost:8030/formats/parse &
sleep 3; curl -m 8 http://localhost:8030/health  → HTTP 000 (repeated 3x). Health returns 200 again only after OCR finishes.
confirmed.fix: Wrap every parser invocation in `await run_in_threadpool(...)` (or make parse sync and call it via `fastapi.concurrency.run_in_threadpool`), and move the OCR/PDF paths to a Celery task the way LLM conversion already is. Also require authentication (or a strict per-IP budget) on /formats/parse since it performs the same expensive extraction as /formats/upload.
confirmed.correction:
Corrected claim: `/formats/parse` (format_routes.py:311) and `/formats/upload` (format_routes.py:386, which parses before its 401 auth gate) run Tesseract OCR and pdfplumber extraction synchronously on the event-loop thread; there is no `run_in_threadpool`/`run_in_executor` anywhere in backend/app. Measured: one unauthenticated 657 KB PNG upload stalled /health for 11 s.

Three corrections to the claimed impact:
1. `/formats/detect/validate` is not a route. The real routes are `/formats/detect` and `/formats/validate`, and NEITHER calls `parse()` — `/formats/validate` (format_routes.py:182) only calls the cheap sync `parser.validate()` (a lazy `Image.open`), and `/formats/detect` only does magic-byte detection. Those two endpoints are not OCR vectors.
2. "The whole FastAPI process unresponsive" holds for a single-worker process (dev: `uvicorn` with no --workers; backend/Dockerfile:51). Production runs `--workers 4` (backend/Dockerfile.prod:69), so one request stalls one of four workers; roughly 4 concurrent uploads are needed to stall the whole service — still trivially within the 60 req/min limit, so the DoS conclusion survives, just not from literally one request in prod.
3. The ~300 s figure is a theoretical worst case (10 pages x 30 s tesseract timeout, plus pdf2image render time) and requires a PDF where pdfplumber extracts zero text. For images the per-request stall is bounded at ~30 s by OCR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS; typical observed stall was ~12 s.

Severity: real, medium-to-high. Fix: wrap the parser bodies (or the call sites) in `starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool` / `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, or better, move OCR/PDF extraction into the existing Celery pipeline instead of doing it inline in the request.

confirmed.title: /formats/upload burns a platform LLM call with no entitlement, quota, or trial gate
confirmed.evidence:
The route signature is `async def upload_for_conversion(file, source_hint, source_platform, user_id = Depends(get_current_user_optional), db = Depends(get_db))` — there is no `dependencies=[Depends(require_feature(...))]` and no trial consumption. `rg -l "entitlement|quota" backend/app` lists 30 route modules; format_routes.py is not one of them. There is no matching key in `backend/app/core/feature_registry.py` (no `import`/`document_conversion` FeatureDef). The handler ends with:
    user_api_key = await api_key_service.get_user_provider(db, user_id, "openai")
    submit_document_conversion(...)
and converter_worker.py:58 `api_key = user_api_key or settings.OPENAI_API_KEY`.
confirmed.impact: Any authenticated free-plan user can POST unlimited PDFs/DOCX/JSON and each one dispatches a gpt-4o-mini completion billed to the platform key when the user has no BYOK. Every comparable LLM route (/optimize, /ai/*, /ats/deep) is gated with `require_feature*` and trial tracking; document import is not, so it is a straightforward bypass of the new entitlement engine and of the admin kill-switch (there is no key to switch off).
confirmed.repro: Read format_routes.py:334-444 — no require_feature dependency, no trial_service call, no usage row written. Contrast with app/api/routes.py:552 `dependencies=[Depends(require_feature_optional("llm_optimize"))]`.
confirmed.fix: Add a `document_import` FeatureDef to feature_registry.py, gate the route with `Depends(require_feature("document_import"))`, and consume the same trial/usage counter the other LLM paths use before calling `submit_document_conversion`.
confirmed.correction: Corrected claim: /formats/upload is the only LLM-dispatching route not represented in backend/app/core/feature_registry.py, so document import cannot be disabled by the admin kill-switch or restricted per plan family the way /optimize, /ai/*, and /ats/deep can. Severity low-to-medium (entitlement-coverage/observability gap), not high. It is NOT an unmetered billing bypass: the route already requires authentication (401 for anonymous, format_routes.py:402-407), is subject to the default 60/min + 1000/hr per-session rate limiter, and caps uploads at 10 MB. The "no quota / no trial consumption" framing is misleading — the codebase has no per-user LLM quota system at all, and the trial mechanism is anonymous-only, so already-gated peers such as /optimize have exactly the same platform-key exposure for authenticated free users. Fix is to add a FeatureDef (e.g. "document_import") and a require_feature dependency for parity, not to plug a live cost leak.

curl -F "file=@big.md" http://localhost:8030/formats/upload → HTTP 413, body `{..."File size exceeds maximum allowed size of 1.0MB for markdown files"...}` (contains no "413").

Corrections to the finding: (a) the 500/502/503 branch is dead too; (b) the lost 413/415 copy is not a big user-visible regression because MultiFormatUpload already pre-validates extension and per-format size client-side, so those statuses rarely reach the server from that path; (c) the genuinely unhandled cases are 401 (no branch exists; hit by every anonymous non-LaTeX upload on /try) and 422 parse failures, which is where the raw JSON actually leaks; (d) an additional bug the finding missed: because request_id is a hex UUID, `message.includes('413'|'415'|'422'|'500')` can match by coincidence and display a misleading friendly message for an unrelated error. Fix is to propagate `response.status` (throw a typed error carrying status + parsed `error.message`) and map on the numeric status, adding a 401 case. Severity is closer to low-medium (cosmetic/UX plus request_id disclosure, which is a correlation id, not a secret).

confirmed.title: Client-side size limits are looser than the server's for five formats

confirmed.impact: A 1.5 MB .md/.txt/.json/.yaml/.toml passes the client validation, is uploaded, and then fails server-side with a 413 that (per the finding above) is rendered as a raw JSON blob. confirmed.title: OAuth callbacks are unauthenticated and never bind the state nonce to the completing browser session — account-linking CSRF on all four integrations
confirmed.evidence:
async def github_callback(
    code: str = Query(...),
    state: str = Query(""),
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
):
    ...
    # Validate the nonce — prevents CSRF account-binding attacks
    user_id = await cache_manager.get(f"gh:oauth:{state}")
    if not user_id:
        return _github_error_redirect("invalid_state")
    ...
    await db.execute(
        update(User)
        .where(User.id == user_id)
        .values(github_access_token=encrypted_token, github_username=username)
    )

Verified there is no auth dependency on any of the four callbacks: `rg 'async def .*_callback' -A 6` shows only `code`, `state`/`oauth_verifier` and `db = Depends(get_db)` — no `get_current_user_required`, no comparison of the session user against the state-bound `user_id`.
confirmed.impact: The comment claims the nonce prevents CSRF account-binding, but it only prevents the *forward* direction. The reverse attack works: the attacker calls `/github/connect` while logged in as themselves, captures their own `state` nonce from the GitHub authorize URL, then sends the victim `https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&state=<attacker_nonce>&redirect_uri=<our callback>`. Because the state is bound to the attacker's `user_id` in Redis and the callback ignores whose browser arrived, the victim's GitHub `code` is exchanged and the victim's `repo`-scoped access token is written onto the ATTACKER's `users` row. The attacker then uses `/github/resumes/{id}/enable` (which accepts an arbitrary `repo_name`) and `/github/resumes/{id}/push` to write commits into the victim's private repositories, and `/pull` to read them. Because `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` is shared with Better Auth social login (see separate finding), any victim who signed up with GitHub has already granted consent, so GitHub redirects silently with no prompt. Identical for Dropbox (`dbx:oauth:{nonce}` → full Dropbox file access), Mendeley (`mendeley:state:{state}`) and Zotero (`zotero:reqsecret:{request_token}`, where the attacker also controls the request token).
confirmed.repro:
1. Attacker (logged in as A) opens `http://localhost:8030/github/connect`, copies the `state=` value from the resulting github.com URL, and aborts.
2. Attacker sends victim B the same authorize URL.
3. B (logged into GitHub, already having authorized the app) is redirected to `http://localhost:8030/github/callback?code=<B's code>&state=<A's nonce>`.
4. `SELECT github_username FROM users WHERE id = A` now shows B's GitHub login; A's `/github/status` reports connected as B.
confirmed.fix: Bind the OAuth handshake to the browser, not just to Redis. In `/connect`, additionally set a short-lived HttpOnly `SameSite=Lax` cookie containing the nonce (or require the callback to carry a valid session), and in the callback resolve the current user via `get_current_user_optional` and reject unless it equals the `user_id` stored under the state key. Do this for all four callbacks; the Zotero flow needs the same treatment keyed on `oauth_token`.
confirmed.correction: The defect is real: all four OAuth callbacks (github/dropbox/mendeley/zotero) are unauthenticated and bind the state nonce only to a user_id in Redis, never to the browser session completing the flow, so a victim's third-party token can be written onto an attacker's user row (CWE-352 account-linking / OAuth token capture). Two claims are overstated: (1) although frontend/src/lib/auth.ts uses the same GITHUB_CLIENT_ID as Better Auth social login, /connect requests scope=repo while social login requests identity scopes, so GitHub will render a consent screen on first repo authorization -- the attack requires the victim to click Authorize (a phishing step), it is not a silent redirect; (2) for Zotero the attacker does not control the request token, Zotero mints it during the attacker's own /connect -- the attacker simply reuses their own token, with the same effect. Fix: bind the nonce to the completing browser (set an HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie containing the nonce at /connect and require it to match at /callback), and/or require an authenticated session on the callback and assert session user_id == nonce-bound user_id.

confirmed.title: Job-scraper rate limit is bypassable with a spoofed X-Forwarded-For header (proven live)
confirmed.impact: `POST /scrape-job-description` is unauthenticated (`get_current_user_optional`) and causes the server to make outbound HTTP requests with retries and a 15s timeout each. The only throttle is this 10/min/IP counter, and any client can rotate the bucket key per request by varying a header it fully controls. `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` exists in `config.py:193` precisely to gate this and is defaulted to `False`, but this endpoint ignores it. Result: unlimited outbound-request amplification / egress-bandwidth abuse from the production IP, plus unbounded growth of `cache:ratelimit:scrape:*` keys in Redis.
confirmed.repro:
Against the running stack:
`for i in $(seq 14); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST localhost:8030/scrape-job-description -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://example.com/job"}'; done`
→ `200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 429 429 429 429`
Then: `for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST localhost:8030/scrape-job-description -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.$i" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://example.com/job"}'; done`
→ `200 200 200` (limit fully bypassed).
confirmed.fix: Replace `_client_ip` with the existing `_spoof_resistant_client_id` from `app/middleware/rate_limiting.py`, which keys on the session token when present and only honours `X-Forwarded-For` when `settings.TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` is true.
confirmed.correction: The bypass is real but the impact is bounded, not unlimited. Because the global RateLimitMiddleware (enabled by default, 60 req/min + 1000 req/hour) covers this path and keys on a spoof-resistant identifier (real peer IP for anonymous callers, ignoring X-Forwarded-For unless TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS is set), a spoofing attacker can only raise their scrape rate from the intended 10/min to the global 60/min / 1000/hour ceiling — roughly 6x, not unbounded egress amplification. Redis key growth is likewise bounded (60s TTL on cache:ratelimit:scrape:* plus the global request ceiling), and the scraper itself blocks private/link-local/metadata targets, caps each fetch at 15s, and caches results 24h. Correct severity is low-to-medium: an inconsistency defect where scraper_routes.py:52-63 should call middleware.rate_limiting._spoof_resistant_client_id instead of its local _client_ip.

confirmed.title: Dropbox per-resume sync state is never returned by the resume API, so the editor's Dropbox Push/Pull controls never appear after a reload
confirmed.evidence:
backend ResumeResponse declares GitHub fields but no Dropbox ones:

    github_sync_enabled: bool = False
    github_repo_name: Optional[str] = None
    github_last_sync_at: Optional[datetime] = None
    created_at: datetime

_resume_response_from_obj() likewise builds only:
        "github_sync_enabled": bool(getattr(resume, "github_sync_enabled", False)),

Frontend reads a field that does not exist:
        // Dropbox sync state (Feature 77)
        setDbxSyncEnabled(data.dropbox_sync_enabled ?? false)
and gates the buttons on it:
              {dbxSyncEnabled && (
                <> ...Push... ...Pull... </>
              )}

Confirmed against the running server's OpenAPI schema: ResumeResponse properties matching github|dropbox = ['github_last_sync_at', 'github_repo_name', 'github_sync_enabled'] — no dropbox_* keys. `rg 'dropbox_sync_enabled' backend/app/api/resume_routes.py` returns nothing.
confirmed.impact: `GET /resumes/{id}` is `response_model=ResumeResponse` (line 774), so Pydantic strips any Dropbox attribute even if present on the ORM object. `data.dropbox_sync_enabled` is therefore always `undefined` and `dbxSyncEnabled` is forced to `false` on every editor load, even though `resumes.dropbox_sync_enabled` is `true` in the database. The Dropbox toggle always renders in the OFF state and the Push/Pull buttons are never rendered — the Dropbox sync feature is unusable after a page refresh. Clicking the toggle again calls `enableDropboxSync`, which silently re-uploads and resets `dropbox_last_sync_at`. GitHub is unaffected because its three fields are present.
confirmed.repro:
1. Connect Dropbox, open a resume, toggle Dropbox sync on (Push/Pull appear).
2. Reload the editor page.
3. Toggle renders OFF and Push/Pull are gone, while `SELECT dropbox_sync_enabled FROM resumes WHERE id=...` is `true`.
confirmed.fix: Add `dropbox_sync_enabled: bool = False`, `dropbox_folder_path: Optional[str] = None`, `dropbox_last_sync_at: Optional[datetime] = None` to `ResumeResponse` and populate them in `_resume_response_from_obj`, mirroring the GitHub fields.
confirmed.correction: Real but medium, not high. Backend ResumeResponse/_resume_response_from_obj omit dropbox_sync_enabled/dropbox_folder_path/dropbox_last_sync_at, and the editor's only load-time initializer (page.tsx:1030) reads that missing field, so dbxSyncEnabled is always false after a reload: the Dropbox toggle renders in the OFF state and Push/Pull stay hidden. However the feature is not unusable — the toggle itself is gated on dbxConnected (fetched separately via GET /dropbox/status) and one click calls enableDropboxSync, which restores Push/Pull for that session. The more precise harm the finding understates is that handleToggleDropboxSync always takes the else/enable branch, so after any reload the user cannot disable sync from the editor and clicking "off" instead re-uploads local content over the Dropbox file and resets dropbox_last_sync_at. No silent server-side data loss occurs because there is no background sync driven by the DB flag (push/pull are explicit endpoints). Fix: add the three dropbox_* fields to ResumeResponse and _resume_response_from_obj, or call the already-implemented but unused apiClient.getResumeDropboxStatus(resumeId) on editor load.

confirmed.title: Every OAuth failure redirect emitted by the backend is silently ignored by the settings page
confirmed.location: frontend/src/app/settings/page.tsx:98-128 vs backend/app/api/github_routes.py:83-87 (and dropbox_routes.py:150-154, zotero_routes.py:202-206, mendeley_routes.py:82-86)

The user gets zero feedback and will retry indefinitely. For Zotero/Mendeley it is worse: the flow was opened in a popup from the References panel, and the error page does not post a message or close, so the popup just sits on a settings page while the parent panel spins on the old state. All the carefully-worded `reason` codes are dead information.
confirmed.repro: Visit `http://localhost:5180/settings?github=error&reason=token_exchange_failed`. The page renders normally with no error shown. Equivalent to what the backend produces after e.g. letting the Redis state nonce expire before approving on GitHub.
confirmed.fix: In the same `useEffect`, add `if (searchParams.get('github') === 'error') setGhError(humanize(searchParams.get('reason')))` for each provider, and for zotero/mendeley also `window.opener.postMessage({type:'zotero:error', reason}, origin)` + `window.close()` so the popup surfaces the failure to the References panel.

Notably the page already declares and renders per-provider error banners (`ghError`/`zotError`/`menError`/`dbxError`, lines 301/369/437/503) fed only by the disconnect handlers, so this is unfinished wiring rather than a missing feature. Confirmed live: `/github/callback?state=bogus&code=x` returns 307 to `/settings?github=error&reason=invalid_state` with no banner shown. For Zotero/Mendeley the popup additionally stays open on a settings page instead of postMessage-ing an error and closing (the parent panel does not hang or spin — it just keeps showing "Connect"). Not part of this defect: consent denial, which arrives as `?error=access_denied` with no `code` and hits the required-`code` query validator, returning raw 422 JSON to the browser — a separate issue worth fixing by making `code` optional and mapping the provider `error` param into the same error redirect.

confirmed.title: Entitlement gate is only on /connect — push, pull, import and status stay fully usable after a plan downgrade
confirmed.impact: `integration_github/dropbox/zotero/mendeley` are paid features in `app/core/feature_registry.py:84-91`, but entitlement is checked once, at connect time, and the resulting token is permanent. A user who subscribes, connects, then downgrades or lets the subscription lapse keeps unlimited GitHub/Dropbox sync and Zotero/Mendeley imports forever — the paywall only delays first use. Secondarily, the settings page renders the four Connect buttons unconditionally with no entitlement check, so a free user clicking Connect gets a full-page raw JSON body from `require_feature`'s `_denied()` (a top-level navigation, not a fetch) instead of an upgrade prompt.
confirmed.repro: Connect GitHub on a paid plan, then set the user's plan to free. `POST /github/resumes/{id}/push` still returns 200 and commits to GitHub. Separately, as a free user click "Connect GitHub" in /settings — the browser navigates to the API and displays the raw 402 JSON error document.
confirmed.fix: Add `dependencies=[Depends(require_feature("integration_x"))]` to the enable/push/pull/import routes as well (leave `/status` and `/disconnect` open so downgraded users can still see and revoke), and gate the Connect buttons in `settings/page.tsx` on the user's entitlements so the paywall is shown in-app.
confirmed.correction: Core issue is real but the framing and severity are wrong. Accurate claim: entitlement enforcement for the four integrations exists only on GET /connect; all value-delivering routes (push, pull, enable, import, collections, status) are ungated, and no code path revokes stored OAuth tokens when an entitlement is withdrawn (Dropbox/Mendeley tokens even auto-refresh). The consequence is that the admin control plane's kill-switch and per-plan matrix toggle cannot actually disable an integration for users who already connected — including as incident-response. It is NOT a paid-feature bypass or revenue leak: backend/alembic/versions/0035_admin_control_plane.py seeds every gateable feature ON for every plan family (free included) and entitlement_service.has_feature fails open, so integrations are currently enabled for everyone and nothing is paywalled. Severity low, not medium. The frontend gap (settings page Connect as top-level navigation with no can() check, yielding a raw JSON 403 page) is real but unreachable today for the same reason.

confirmed.title: Connect buttons authenticate only via the Better Auth cookie on the API origin, while every other API call is Bearer-token-only
confirmed.evidence:
settings/page.tsx does a top-level navigation (no headers possible):
    window.location.href = `${API_BASE}/github/connect`

But apiClient authenticates purely with a localStorage bearer and never sends cookies:
    const token = this.authToken ?? (typeof window !== 'undefined' ? localStorage.getItem('auth_token') : null)
    if (token) h['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`
    ...
    const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE}${path}`, { ...init, headers })   // no credentials: 'include'

Better Auth is configured without any cookie-domain / cross-subdomain setting — `advanced` contains only:
  advanced: {
    database: { generateId: () => crypto.randomUUID() },
  },
so `better-auth.session_token` is a host-only cookie on the Next.js origin.
confirmed.impact: The four `/connect` routes require `get_current_user_required`, which for a browser navigation can only be satisfied by the `better-auth.session_token` cookie (confirmed live: `curl localhost:8030/github/connect` → 401). This works today only because dev runs both the app and the API on `localhost` (cookies ignore port). In any deployment where `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` points at a different host than `BETTER_AUTH_URL` — the normal split-domain setup this config anticipates — the host-only cookie is not sent, and all four Connect buttons dump a raw `{"detail":"Not authenticated"}` 401 page at the user. The rest of the integration UI keeps working (Bearer), which makes the failure look arbitrary.
confirmed.repro: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:8030/github/connect` → 401. Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.example.com` with the app on `https://app.example.com`, sign in, click Connect GitHub → the same 401 JSON page, because the session cookie is scoped to app.example.com only.
confirmed.fix: Either configure Better Auth `advanced.crossSubDomainCookies` with the shared parent domain, or stop relying on the cookie: have `/connect` accept a short-lived one-time connect ticket minted by an authenticated `POST /github/connect-ticket` (Bearer) and passed as a query param on the navigation.
confirmed.correction: Real but narrower than stated. The four /connect routes are reachable only via a top-level browser navigation, and the backend's token extractor supports only a Bearer header or the host-only better-auth.session_token cookie, so these navigations authenticate by cookie-on-the-API-origin alone. This is NOT broken in the project's primary deployment: the released frontend image is built with NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=/api and nginx proxies /api/ to the backend (docker-compose.prod / k8s), making app and API same-origin. It IS broken in the split-host topology the repo itself documents in frontend/.env.production.example (Vercel app host + https://api.your-domain.com), where the host-only cookie is never sent and all four Connect buttons return a raw {"detail":"Not authenticated"} 401 page while the Bearer-based integration calls continue to work. Severity is closer to low/medium (config-dependent latent footgun, not a live break); the fix is to authorize /connect with a short-lived one-time token or to fetch the OAuth authorize URL over an authenticated XHR and redirect client-side.

confirmed.title: SSRF guard resolves DNS separately from the connection, leaving a TOCTOU / DNS-rebinding window to the cloud metadata service
confirmed.impact: The validation resolution and the connection resolution are two separate lookups of an attacker-controlled hostname. An attacker serving a 1-second-TTL record that alternates between a public IP and `169.254.169.254` (or an internal RFC1918 host) passes the check and then connects to the internal address. Because `/scrape-job-description` is unauthenticated and the extracted page body is returned verbatim in `description`, a successful rebind exfiltrates cloud instance-metadata credentials directly in the HTTP response. The guard correctly blocks all the static cases — I confirmed live that `169.254.169.254`, `localhost:8030` and `127.0.0.1:8030` all return `"error":"Invalid or disallowed URL"` — so this is the remaining gap, not a general absence of protection.
confirmed.repro: Point a hostname you control at a rebinding DNS server alternating A records between a public IP and 169.254.169.254 with TTL 0, then `POST /scrape-job-description {"url":"http://rebind.example.com/"}` repeatedly; the guard's lookup and httpx's lookup will eventually disagree.
confirmed.fix: Resolve once in the guard, pick a validated public address, and connect to that IP directly (pass the literal IP in the URL with the original host in the `Host` header and SNI), or install a `socket.getaddrinfo`-level hook / custom connector that re-checks the actual peer address after `connect()`. A destination allowlist for the known job boards would be stronger still.
confirmed.correction:
Corrected claim (severity: low, not medium): The SSRF guard in backend/app/services/job_scraper_service.py performs DNS resolution separately from the connection (_assert_public_url at line 885, _SSRFGuardTransport at lines 81-93, then httpcore's own resolution inside super().handle_async_request), so no validated address is pinned. An attacker controlling authoritative DNS with a short/zero TTL can pass the check and have the actual TCP connection go to an internal address — a real DNS-rebinding window on an unauthenticated endpoint (backend/app/api/scraper_routes.py:86, rate-limited to 10/min/IP).

The impact is blind-to-semi-blind SSRF, NOT cloud-credential exfiltration. Two independent reasons: (1) the response body is not returned verbatim — _extract_generic_html (line 800) only considers div/section/article/main blocks scoring > 2, so JSON/plaintext metadata bodies yield candidates == [] and fall through to og:description == None; verified empirically that an IMDS credentials JSON produces title=None, description=None, source="og_tags", is_useful()=False, and is not cached. (2) the scraper sends only _BROWSER_HEADERS, so AWS IMDSv2 (the default), GCP (Metadata-Flavor) and Azure (Metadata: true) all refuse the request anyway. Content is only recoverable if the internal target serves HTML with sufficiently large div/section/article/main blocks; otherwise the attacker gets an oracle distinguishing reachable internal hosts ("Page unavailable (blocked or not found)" vs. other outcomes).

Recommended fix: resolve the hostname once, then connect to the pinned IP (e.g. pass the literal IP in the URL with an explicit Host header, or override the transport's resolver / use a socket-level connect hook that re-validates the peer address after connect), and re-validate per redirect hop.

confirmed.title: /ws/collab bypasses the LEGACY_JWT_ENABLED kill-switch and accepts self-signed HS256 tokens

confirmed.impact: Revocation is not effective. A collaborator who is removed (or demoted) keeps an open socket that continues to receive every peer update, cursor position and full-document SYNC_STEP2 catch-up, and continues to broadcast and persist their own edits into `collab:{resume_id}:updates` for as long as the socket stays open (no idle timeout exists in the handler). Since the owner UI reports 'Removed X' on a 204, the owner believes access is gone.
confirmed.repro: Owner invites B, B opens the editor (socket established). Owner clicks Remove in CollaboratorPanel (DELETE /resumes/{id}/collaborators/{userId} → 204). B's browser keeps typing: edits still relay to the owner and vice versa until B reloads.

confirmed.correction: Corrected claim (severity: medium, not high): `remove_collaborator` (resume_routes.py:2247-2269) deletes the `resume_collaborators` row but has no way to signal the in-process `collab_manager`, and `collab_websocket` (ws_routes.py:243-357) authorizes only once before `accept()` with no per-message or periodic re-check. A collaborator who is removed while already connected keeps full read/write access on that existing socket — receiving peer updates and full `SYNC_STEP2` catch-up, and having their own edits persisted to `collab:{resume_id}:updates` — until the socket closes. The window is bounded, not unbounded: any reconnect (tab reload, network blip, or y-websocket's ~30s no-message client-side close, which fires whenever peers are idle since the server sends no keepalives and excludes the sender from broadcasts) re-runs the check and yields 4003. So the exposure is "revocation is not immediate for an already-open session, and can persist indefinitely while peers keep editing", not "revocation is not effective". Separately, role demotion is not part of this bug: the collab WS handler never reads `ResumeCollaborator.role`, so a `viewer` has write access even on a fresh connection — file that as its own finding. Any fix must go through Redis pub/sub, since `CollabManager` rooms are per-process in-memory.

confirmed.title: Real-time collaboration cannot work in production: CollabManager rooms are process-local while prod runs 4 uvicorn workers
confirmed.impact: `_rooms` and `_clients` live in one Python process. Two users editing the same resume land on different uvicorn workers with probability 3/4 and will never see each other's Y.js updates or cursors — `room.broadcast` only iterates locally-connected sockets and there is no Redis pub/sub relay (Redis is used only for the join-time catch-up list). Both sides silently diverge and each one's edits overwrite the other on the next save. Contrast /ws/jobs, which correctly fans out through `event_bus` over Redis pub/sub.
confirmed.repro: Run the prod image (4 workers). Open the same resume in two browsers as owner + collaborator. Typing in one produces no cursor/character updates in the other; reloading pulls a partial merge from the Redis update list.
confirmed.fix: Relay collab frames through Redis pub/sub (channel `collab:{resume_id}`) exactly like event_bus does for jobs, with each worker forwarding received messages to its local room, or pin collab to a single process/sticky routing.
confirmed.correction: CollabManager rooms are genuinely process-local with no Redis relay, so live collaboration breaks on any multi-process deployment (Dockerfile.prod: 4 uvicorn workers; docker-compose.prod.yml: 3 replicas => up to 12 processes, nginx least_conn with no sticky routing). Corrected impact: peers on different processes see no live remote edits and no cursors/presence, and whichever client saves last overwrites the other's DB content from its stale buffer. However, the CRDT log itself is NOT corrupted or divergent — both processes append updates to the same Redis key collab:{resume_id}:updates, and any client that reconnects/refreshes replays the full log via _send_catchup and Y.js merges both peers' edits. Severity medium-high rather than high, further tempered by the fact that the cited prod compose/nginx config could not route collab traffic as written (uvicorn binds :8000 vs upstream backend:8030; no nginx location for /ws/collab), i.e. that deployment path looks unexercised.

confirmed.impact: Workbox matches RegExp routes against the absolute `url.href`. `/^\/(_next...)/ ` is anchored to a literal leading slash, which never occurs in 'https://host/_next/static/...', so the `latexy-app-shell` StaleWhileRevalidate route never fires. Consequently: (1) `/^\/(_next\/static|_next\/image)/` (line 46) can never match, so the `latexy-app-shell` StaleWhileRevalidate route never fires — but this is largely benign because the generated precache manifest in public/sw.js already precaches all 81 /_next/static assets; the only real loss is /_next/image responses. (2) `/\/resumes($|\?)/` (line 54) never matches the actual list request `${API_BASE}/resumes/?page=1&limit=20` (api-client.ts:1047/1054) because '/resumes' is followed by '/', so the `latexy-api-resumes` NetworkFirst route never fires and offline users get /offline.html instead of a cached resume list. (3) Additionally (missed by the finding) `/\.pdf$/` only works for same-origin PDFs; cross-origin MinIO/S3 PDF URLs fail the index===0 cross-origin check, so the documented 'MinIO PDF assets -> CacheFirst' behaviour also does not apply. frontend/src/sw-config.ts (not src/lib/sw-config.ts) is unimported documentation whose resumeApi pattern differs from the shipped one and is broken identically. Of the 34 files containing a `fixed inset-0 z-` overlay, only 6 declare role="dialog" (KeyboardShortcutsPanel.tsx:64, DiffViewerModal.tsx:285, SemanticMatchModal.tsx:60, ConfidenceScorePanel.tsx:123, SalaryEstimatorPanel.tsx:88, ats/DeepAnalysisPanel.tsx:177) and 14 contain no 'Escape' string at all (ApplyModal.tsx, GenerateReferencesModal.tsx, ExportDropdown.tsx, WatermarkDownloadPopover.tsx, MacroLibraryPanel.tsx, SectionReorderPanel.tsx, ContactFormatterPanel.tsx, DateStandardizerPanel.tsx, AgeAnalysisPanel.tsx, CompileErrorHistory.tsx, byok/APIKeyManager.tsx, admin/tenant/page.tsx, ats/SemanticMatchModal.tsx, ExportDropdown.tsx).

SemanticMatchModal is the worst case: it declares role="dialog" aria-modal="true" — which tells assistive tech the background is inert — while providing neither a trap nor an Escape key. Nothing restores focus to the trigger on close anywhere in the app.
confirmed.repro: Open /workspace/<id>/edit, open the Export dropdown or any ATS panel, press Escape (nothing happens), then press Tab repeatedly — focus walks into the toolbar and editor behind the overlay.
confirmed.fix: Introduce one shared <Modal> primitive (or adopt @radix-ui/react-dialog, already a transitive dep via react-slot) that provides role=dialog + aria-modal + aria-labelledby, an Escape handler, a focus trap, and focus restore, then migrate the 34 overlays onto it.
